name: Thrash Metal
about: Thrash metal fused the speed of Motörhead and the NWOBHM with hardcore punk's aggression, and it was born in the San Francisco Bay Area and Los Angeles in 1983, when Metallica's Kill 'Em All and Slayer's Show No Mercy arrived within months of each other. Its signature is the palm-muted, down-picked riff at punk tempo, barked vocals, double-bass drumming and lyrics about war, politics and the end of the world. The Big Four of Metallica, Slayer, Megadeth and Anthrax had taken it to arenas by 1991, while a German school led by Kreator and Sodom and Brazil's Sepultura pushed it toward death metal. It collapsed under grunge and groove metal in the mid-1990s, and a 2000s revival around Evile, Municipal Waste and Vektor keeps it running.

artists.name: Slayer
artists.why: the fastest and most extreme of the Big Four

artists.name: Megadeth
artists.why: Dave Mustaine's technical, bitter rival camp

artists.name: Exodus
artists.why: Bay Area originators, the scene's Bonded by Blood

artists.name: Testament
artists.why: the Bay Area's most durable second-wave band

artists.name: Dark Angel
artists.why: the fastest thrash in Los Angeles

albums.title: Ride the Lightning
albums.why: Fade to Black, Creeping Death and the instrumental Call of Ktulu show thrash growing up fast, adding dynamics and melody without losing any speed.

albums.title: Bonded by Blood
albums.why: Delayed a year by label trouble, the Bay Area's founding thrash document still arrived with Paul Baloff's bark and riffs Kirk Hammett had helped write.

albums.title: Seven Churches
albums.why: Teenage thrash from San Francisco so fast and Satanic that it is often called the first death metal album; it closes with a song of that name.

albums.title: Infernal Overkill
albums.why: Schmier's shriek and Mike Sifringer's riffs on the first full-length of the German Big Three, raw and formative rather than fully realised.

albums.title: Peace Sells... but Who's Buying?
albums.why: Mustaine's jazz-inflected riffs, the bassline MTV News borrowed and a sour wit set Megadeth apart from the band that had fired him.

albums.title: Master of Puppets
albums.why: Eight songs of thrash composed like symphonies, with the title track and Orion as evidence that the genre could carry real scale and grief.

albums.title: Reign in Blood
albums.why: From Angel of Death to Raining Blood in under half an hour, produced bone-dry by Rick Rubin; the extreme-metal benchmark that nothing has moved.

albums.title: Pleasure to Kill
albums.why: Mille Petrozza's Essen band at their most violent, the German thrash album that mattered most to the death metal bands forming across Europe and Florida.

albums.title: Darkness Descends
albums.why: Gene Hoglan's drumming and a tempo that embarrassed its contemporaries on the Los Angeles band's second album, the fastest record of thrash's peak year.

albums.title: Game Over
albums.why: Dan Lilker, fresh from Anthrax, and John Connelly's political New York thrash, short songs and hardcore pace on a scrappy but influential debut.

albums.title: Among the Living
albums.why: Caught in a Mosh, Indians and I Am the Law made Anthrax's third album their defining one, thrash with gang vocals and a sense of humour.

albums.title: The Legacy
albums.why: Alex Skolnick's leads and Chuck Billy's roar on the strongest Bay Area debut after Exodus, with Over the Wall as its signature.

albums.title: The Ultra-Violence
albums.why: Recorded when the drummer was fourteen, the Filipino-American cousins' debut is one of the most athletic and musical thrash records of the Bay Area's golden year.

albums.title: Dimension Hatröss
albums.why: Piggy's dissonant chords and a science-fiction concept took Voivod from thrash toward progressive rock, the point where the band became unique.

albums.title: South of Heaven
albums.why: Slayer slowed down after Reign in Blood and found that their riffs were just as frightening at half speed, with Mandatory Suicide and the title track to prove it.

albums.title: Eternal Nightmare
albums.why: Sean Killian's manic vocals and Robb Flynn's riffs, before Machine Head, on the Bay Area's most hyperactive thrash album.

albums.title: Agent Orange
albums.why: Tom Angelripper's Vietnam-themed thrash, with Frank Blackfire's guitar at its sharpest, the German school's best-produced and most complete album.

albums.title: Beneath the Remains
albums.why: Produced by Scott Burns in Rio, the Cavalera brothers' breakthrough brought Brazilian thrash to the world with Inner Self and the title track.

albums.title: The Years of Decay
albums.why: Terry Date's production and Bobby Blitz's snarl on Overkill's most varied album, with Elimination and the ten-minute Playing with Spiders.

albums.title: Alice in Hell
albums.why: Jeff Waters played nearly everything on a Canadian debut whose riffing precision and Alison Hell made it a technical thrash landmark.

albums.title: Rust in Peace
albums.why: Holy Wars... The Punishment Due and Hangar 18, with Marty Friedman's leads and Nick Menza's drums, the technical peak of the whole Big Four.

albums.title: Arise
albums.why: Sepultura's thrash at its tightest, a hair before groove and tribal rhythm took over, with Dead Embryonic Cells and the title song as its spine.

albums.title: Mental Vortex
albums.why: The Swiss trio's most refined album, technical thrash with jazz and classical shading and a Beatles cover that somehow fits.

albums.title: Epidemic of Violence
albums.why: New York thrash at death metal intensity, released as the genre was collapsing and treasured since as its most brutal late statement.

albums.title: Enter the Grave
albums.why: Produced by Flemming Rasmussen of Metallica fame, the Huddersfield band's debut led the British thrash revival with unapologetic 1986 worship.

albums.title: Terminal Redux
albums.why: A seventy-minute science-fiction concept with choirs and Voivod-style chords, the most ambitious record the thrash revival has produced.
